passage:
"Mummy, Karan said my hair looks like a bird's nest." Ira, five, sat on the bed and would not look up. Her mother Pema sat beside her.
"How did that feel?"
"Sad. I didn't want to go on the swing after."
"Thank you for telling me. Words like that can hurt, and it's not okay to say them. Did you say anything to Karan?"
"I said stop."
"Good. Shall we tell Miss tomorrow together?"
"Yes."

qa.q: What did Karan say about Ira's hair?
qa.a: That it looks like a bird's nest.

qa.q: How was Ira feeling after Karan's comment, and what shows it?
qa.a: Sad. She did not want to go on the swing afterwards and would not look up.

qa.q: What did Pema suggest doing?
qa.a: Telling Miss together the next day.

qa.q: How might Karan have seen the remark?
qa.a: Perhaps as a joke, without realising it hurt.

grounding: Shows a child recognising that a teasing remark hurt and telling a trusted adult.

passage: Note from Jagdish, class teacher. Preeti (5) came to me at snack holding her lunchbox tight. "Yash said I'm stupid and he won't be my friend." Her voice was small and she would not look up. I thanked her for telling me. I said "stupid" is not okay to say and that she is not stupid. I spoke to Yash separately, and we practised words for when he is cross. Preeti stayed near me a while, then went to play. I will check in tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Preeti hold tightly?
qa.a: Her lunchbox.

qa.q: How might Preeti be feeling, and what is the evidence?
qa.a: Hurt and perhaps a little afraid of losing a friend, shown by her small voice and not looking up. She may also be embarrassed.

qa.q: What did Jagdish do that helped?
qa.a: Jagdish thanked her, said the word is not okay and she is not stupid, and spoke to Yash separately.

qa.q: How might Yash have felt when Jagdish spoke to him?
qa.a: Perhaps embarrassed or still cross, since they practised words for when he is cross.

grounding: Shows a young child who was hurt by an insult telling a trusted teacher, who takes it seriously.

passage: Behind the village school, Karthik, a bigger boy, told Payal, “You can't play. You smell like cow dung.” The others laughed. Then he leaned close. “If you tell, I'll push you in the ditch.” Payal walked away, her throat tight. At home she didn't eat. Her grandmother asked, “What's wrong, beti?” Payal told her everything. Dadi held her. “Those words were unkind and that was a threat. You were right to tell me.” That afternoon Dadi walked to the school and spoke to the headmaster, who called Karthik's parents.

qa.q: What did Karthik threaten to do if Payal told?
qa.a: Push her in the ditch.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling when she walked away with a tight throat?
qa.a: She was hurt and ashamed by the laughter, and scared because of the threat.

qa.q: What did Dadi do that a trusted adult should do?
qa.a: She listened, told Payal she was right to tell, and went to the headmaster that same afternoon.

qa.q: How might the other children who laughed see it later?
qa.a: They might realise the words made Payal sad and scared, and that laughing along was unkind.

grounding: A child learns that teasing and threats are not okay, tells her grandmother, and her grandmother acts the same day.

passage: In the kindergarten in Hamburg, Felix lost at the counting game and shouted at Nadia, “You're stupid! Stupid!” Nadia's chin wobbled and she hid behind the curtain. Felix stopped. He hadn't expected that. The teacher came and sat by Felix. “Look at Nadia. How do you think she feels?” “Sad,” Felix mumbled. “Some words hurt, like a push inside. ‘Stupid’ is one. What could you say when you lose?” “‘I'm cross.’” He went to the curtain. “Sorry, Nadia. I was cross.” She peeked out.

qa.q: Where did Nadia hide?
qa.a: Behind the curtain.

qa.q: What was Felix feeling when he stopped after Nadia hid?
qa.a: He was surprised and uneasy, realising that his words had made Nadia sad.

qa.q: What did the teacher help Felix learn?
qa.a: That some words hurt like a push inside, and that he could say “I'm cross” instead when he loses.

qa.q: How did Nadia experience Felix's shouted words?
qa.a: They hurt and scared her, so she hid behind the curtain.

grounding: A child learns that insults make others sad, and his teacher helps him use kinder words.

passage: At the community centre lunch, two older boys held their noses at Chaitanya's tiffin. “Smelly food! Smelly boy!” Chaitanya put the lid back on and stopped eating. He went to Trisha, the centre helper. “They said I'm smelly. I don't want my lunch.” Trisha knelt. “Thank you for telling me. That was unkind, and it's not okay. Your food smells yummy.” She sat with him to eat, then talked to the older boys straight after lunch and phoned Chaitanya's mother that evening.

qa.q: What did the older boys hold at Chaitanya's tiffin?
qa.a: Their noses.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling when he put the lid back on?
qa.a: He felt hurt and ashamed of his lunch because of the teasing.

qa.q: What did Trisha do after Chaitanya told her?
qa.a: She thanked him, said the teasing was not okay, sat with him to eat, spoke to the boys after lunch and phoned his mother that evening.

qa.q: How might the older boys see their teasing after Trisha talks to them?
qa.a: They may realise their joke made Chaitanya sad and ashamed, and that such words are not okay.

grounding: A child is teased about his food, recognises it hurt, tells a trusted adult, and she acts the same day.

passage:
I'm Mohit, and I sit behind Hemant in the school van. This morning a big boy from Class 4 leaned over and said, "Move, baby-face, or I'll throw your bag out the window."

Hemant went very quiet. His chin wobbled and he held his bag tight. I said, "That's not okay to say."

When we got to school, Hemant went straight to our class teacher and told her. She listened, thanked him, and went to find the big boy before assembly. She told the van aunty too.

On the way home, the big boy sat at the front and said sorry to Hemant.

qa.q: What did the big boy threaten to do?
qa.a: Throw Hemant's bag out the window.

qa.q: What was Hemant probably feeling when he went quiet and held his bag tight?
qa.a: He was most likely scared and hurt by the name-calling and the threat; his wobbling chin shows he was close to tears. He may also have felt small next to the bigger boy.

qa.q: Which choices were wise here?
qa.a: Mohit said the words were not okay, and Hemant told a trusted adult; the teacher acted that same morning by speaking to the big boy and telling the van aunty.

qa.q: How might the big boy come to see his words after the teacher speaks to him?
qa.a: He may realise that calling someone baby-face and threatening them made a younger child scared, which is why he says sorry on the way home.

grounding: It shows a young child hurt and frightened by an insult and a threat, a classmate naming it as not okay, and the child telling a trusted adult who acts the same day.
